title: Close an attempt that never reattaches and allow one successor
description:
Split out of task-58f7db9a9e44469e9351b2cdea73b47d on 2026-09-11 with operator approval: that card needed 10 files, the size gate's hard ceiling. The sibling keeps the restart hold and the reattach surface, which is what its acceptance case drives. This card owns the give-up half, which that acceptance case does not exercise, and carries two definition-of-done items moved verbatim from it.

Objective: an attempt that is parked in the reconciling phase must not stay there forever. A runner confirmed dead, or one that never comes back within a bounded window, has to release the task for exactly one more execution.

Deliverable: a reconcile-window sweep in packages/moe-daemon/src/state/sweeps.ts, beside the existing sweeps, that closes a reconciling attempt once it is confirmed dead or has sat unreattached past the window, and permits exactly one successor generation for its task. The window is a settings key in .moe/project.json with a documented default, resolved in packages/moe-daemon/src/index.ts where the other timeouts are, and documented in docs/CONFIGURATION.md.

The window is a bound on RECONCILING ONLY. It must never be consulted for an attempt that is running, including one that has successfully reattached, because that would be an idle-based auto-release for WORKING or PLANNING through the back door. The existing rule stands: a quiet build is not evidence of a dead worker, and REVIEW's reviewStaleTimeoutMs self-heal is untouched.

Not in scope: daemon startup reconciliation, the reattach tool and the claim hold, all of which belong to task-58f7db9a9e44469e9351b2cdea73b47d; heartbeat presence kinds, which are task-06b658be6e2c4b4bbfaab2f7f200e1f5.

Verification: npx vitest run src/state/sweeps.test.ts src/state/workerStore.test.ts from packages/moe-daemon.
definitionOfDone: An attempt confirmed dead, or unreattached past the configurable reconcile window, is closed and permits exactly one successor generation
The reconcile window is a settings key with a documented default and is never applied to a live reattached attempt, so no idle-based auto-release is introduced for WORKING or PLANNING
The successor is exactly one: a closed reconciling attempt yields a single next generation and a repeated sweep pass opens no further attempt, proven by a test
The sweep leaves a running or successfully reattached attempt untouched regardless of how long it has been quiet, proven by a test that fails on a window check applied to the running phase
docs/CONFIGURATION.md documents the key, its default and the fact that it bounds reconciling only
npx vitest run src/state/sweeps.test.ts src/state/workerStore.test.ts passes and npm test in packages/moe-daemon stays green
taskRails: Do not reintroduce idle-based auto-release for WORKING or PLANNING; the window bounds the reconciling phase only.
REVIEW's existing reviewStaleTimeoutMs self-heal stays exactly as it is.
Reassignment must establish the old process stopped, or contain its writes; a JSON record alone does not stop a running CLI.

implementationPlan.description: READ THE THREE IDIOMS THIS SWEEP MUST COPY, AND SETTLE THE CONFIRMED-DEAD ARM (read-only, no edits). Read packages/moe-daemon/src/state/sweeps.ts end to end. Every sweep there follows one shape: a `startXCheck(state, intervalMs)` that stores its handle on the state and creates the timer through `state.mutex.exit(() => setInterval(...))`, a matching `stopXCheck(state)`, and a separately exported async `checkX`/`runXSweep` that a test can call directly without any timer. Copy that shape exactly; the mutex-exit wrapper is not optional, because a timer created inside the mutex context inherits it and its callback would then run unlocked. Read `runBlockedTimeoutSweep` around line 213 for how a sweep releases a task, and note it routes through `nextStatusForRelease` rather than writing a status by hand. Read the settings seam: the option field on StateManagerOptions near line 345, its constructor default near line 436, and `applyProjectSettings` near line 1079, which is what reads `.moe/project.json`. Read how `blockedTimeoutMs` and `reviewStaleTimeoutMs` flow through all three, and read the settings table row for `reviewStaleTimeoutMs` in docs/CONFIGURATION.md around line 177 for the documentation format. In the attempt store, confirm what `OPEN_PHASES` at line 44 contains and that `setAttemptPhase` treats closed as terminal and a repeated phase as a no-op. NOW SETTLE THE FIRST DEFINITION-OF-DONE ITEM, whose confirmed-dead arm has no implementation in this card by design: an epic rail keeps the daemon state-only and forbids it from running processes, so the daemon cannot itself establish that a runner died. The only authority that can is the wrapper's exit trap calling `moe.deregister_worker`, and the attempt-lifecycle work already closes the attempt it owns on that path. Verify that by reading the deregister close path and confirming it closes a reconciling attempt, not just a running one. Record the finding in the step note: the confirmed-dead arm is the existing deregister path, and what this card adds is the bounded window for the case where no such declaration ever arrives. Produce no diff in this step.
implementationPlan.note:
READ-ONLY. No diff. Findings:

CONFIRMED-DEAD ARM IS ALREADY IMPLEMENTED — verified, not assumed. `deregisterWorker` (state/workerLifecycle.ts:174) -> `releaseWorkerTasks` (:120) -> per task `closeOpenAttempts(state, task.id)` (:146). `closeOpenAttempts` (state/attemptStore.ts:321) iterates `listAttempts` and closes every attempt whose phase is in `OPEN_PHASES` — and `OPEN_PHASES` (attemptStore.ts:44) is exactly {running, finalizing, reconciling}. So a RECONCILING attempt IS closed on the deregister path, not just a running one. Epic rail keeps the daemon state-only, so the wrapper's exit trap calling moe.deregister_worker is the only authority that can declare a process dead; this card adds the bounded window for when no such declaration ever arrives.

SWEEP SHAPE: all three sweeps use `state.mutex.exit(() => setInterval(...))` + `.unref()`, handle stored on state (`blockedTimeoutInterval`/`proposalPurgeInterval`/`staleWorkerInterval`), matching `stopX(state)`, and a separately exported async body a test calls with no timer. `runBlockedTimeoutSweep` (sweeps.ts:213) releases via `state.updateTask(id, { assignedWorkerId: null, status: nextStatusForRelease(owned, ctx) }, 'WORKER_TIMEOUT')`.

RELEASE CONTEXT CORRECTION: the blocked sweep passes 'park' -> BACKLOG (human triage). BACKLOG is human-gated and invisible to agents, so 'park' would NOT let a successor claim. This card must use the DEFAULT 'requeue' context: `nextStatusForRelease` (workerLifecycle.ts:76) maps WORKING -> WORKING-unassigned (or REVIEW when every step is done), which is exactly the column a successor claims from.

SETTINGS SEAM (5 sites, two more than the plan named): StateManagerOptions field :343-355; public field :414-416 + `*Explicit` flag :421-422; constructor default :436-442; `applySettingsTimeouts` :1084-1096 (the plan called it `applyProjectSettings` — that name does not exist); AND `ProjectSettings` in types/schema.ts:197 for the typed read, plus persistence.ts:123 `normalizeProject` sanitize. normalizeProject spreads `...project.settings` first, so an unsanitized new key still survives a load/normalize/write cycle. docs/CONFIGURATION.md row format at :177 (`| key | what it bounds | Milliseconds (default: N = human) |`).

INDEX.TS DOES NOT WIRE SWEEPS OR TIMEOUTS — plan premise does not match the code. `src/index.ts:500` is `new StateManager({ projectPath })` with NO timeout options; its only timeout constants are process-level env vars (SOCKET/PORT_READY/LOCK_STALE/SHUTDOWN/HTTP_CLOSE). All three sweep lifecycles are armed in `StateManager.load()` :1073-1075 (deliberately OUTSIDE the locked section — an interval armed inside inherits the mutex ALS context and every tick runs unlocked) and stopped in `clearEmitter()` :457-460. Step 4 will therefore arm/stop the new sweep there, which IS "alongside the other sweep lifecycles"; adding a second arming path in index.ts would duplicate it. Called out here so step 6 and QA do not read the untouched index.ts as a missed requirement.

ATTEMPT STORE NEEDS NO CHANGE: `setAttemptPhase` (:221) returns the record unchanged when the phase already equals the target (no write, lastPhaseAt untouched) and refuses any transition out of `closed` with ATTEMPT_CLOSED; `lastPhaseAt` is the timestamp of the phase CHANGE, which is the clock this window must read. Generation allocator `nextGeneration` (:99) takes max over EVERY prior attempt including closed ones, and `assertNoOpenAttempt` (:160) refuses a second open attempt — together they are the single-successor guarantee, so the sweep needs no counter. `claim_next_task` opens the successor via `openClaimAttempt` (claimNextTask.ts:40) and returns `{ attemptId, generation }` beside `task`.

Dirty paths belonging to other sessions, untouched: packages/moe-daemon/src/tools/createTask.{ts,test.ts} plus several .moe/tasks/*.json and .moe/epics, .moe/resources.

implementationPlan.description: WRITE THE FAILING TESTS FIRST AND CAPTURE RED PROOF. Create packages/moe-daemon/src/state/sweeps.test.ts using the existing ToolTestHarness convention, calling the exported sweep function directly rather than waiting on a timer, and controlling time by writing the attempt's phase timestamp into the past rather than by sleeping. Cover, with exact assertions: an attempt in the reconciling phase whose phase timestamp is older than the window is closed, asserted as the exact phase string, and its task is released so a successor can claim it; the same attempt one millisecond inside the window is left completely alone, proving the boundary is a real comparison and not an always-fire; an attempt in the RUNNING phase is untouched no matter how old its timestamp or how long its worker has been quiet, which is the case that fails if anyone applies the window to a live or reattached attempt; an attempt in the FINALIZING phase is likewise untouched, because its bound belongs to the landing path and not to this window; a second sweep pass over an already-closed attempt writes nothing and opens nothing, which is what makes the successor exactly one; and after the sweep exactly one claim succeeds and receives the next generation while a second concurrent claim is refused, proving the single-successor rule comes from the store's exclusivity rather than from anything the sweep does. Add one case asserting the sweep measures from the attempt's own phase timestamp and never from the worker's last activity: seed a worker quiet for hours with a reconciling attempt that entered the phase seconds ago and assert nothing happens. Run `npx vitest run src/state/sweeps.test.ts` from packages/moe-daemon and SAVE the failing output as the epic rail's fails-on-old-behaviour evidence — on today's code the sweep does not exist, so record which import or symbol is missing. 9 cases, all calling the exported sweep directly with a PINNED clock — no timer, no sleeping. The sweep signature the tests drive is `checkReconcileWindow(state, nowMs = Date.now())`, mirroring `purgeResolvedProposals(state, nowMs = Date.now())` already in this file. Passing `nowMs` is load-bearing for the boundary case: with a wall-clock `Date.now()` inside the sweep, a fixture seeded at `WINDOW - 1` flakes the moment a millisecond elapses between seeding and sweeping. Time is controlled only by writing the attempt's `lastPhaseAt` into the past.

Cases:
1. reconciling at WINDOW+1 -> closed. Exact phase string `'closed'` in the map AND in the on-disk record; task released to `status: 'WORKING'`, `assignedWorkerId: null` (the routing's requeue column, not BACKLOG).
2. reconciling at WINDOW-1 -> untouched, asserted as a whole-record `toEqual` against the seeded object (byte-identity), so an always-fire sweep fails here.
3. running at WINDOW*10 with a worker quiet 3h -> untouched, whole-record equality, task still assigned. This is the case that fails if anyone applies the window to a live or reattached attempt.
4. finalizing at WINDOW*10 -> untouched, same assertions.
5. CLOCK SOURCE: worker `lastActivityAt` 3h old, attempt entered reconciling 5s ago -> nothing happens, and the worker's `lastActivityAt` is asserted unchanged. A sweep reading worker idle releases this row.
6. repeated pass over an already-closed attempt at NOW+WINDOW*10: returns [], whole attempt record equal, FILE MTIME equal (proves no rewrite, not just no semantic change), task record equal, and `listAttempts(task).length` still 1 — the sweep opens nothing.
7. exactly one successor: after the sweep one claim succeeds with `generation: 2` (never a reissued 1); a second claim answers `hasNext: false`; a direct `openAttempt` for the same task is refused `ATTEMPT_ALREADY_OPEN`, which is the store-level proof that the single-successor rule is the store's and not a counter in the sweep; final state `generations [1,2]` / `phases ['closed','running']`.
8. per-record tolerance: two past-window reconciling attempts, `writeEntity` stubbed to throw for one of them; the other is still closed and released, and the failed one is left exactly as it was (still reconciling, still assigned).
9. timer hygiene: `startReconcileWindowCheck` stores a handle on the state, `stopReconcileWindowCheck` calls `clearInterval` with THAT handle and clears the field — an uncleared interval keeps the vitest process alive.

Pick a default generously longer than a realistic daemon restart plus runner relaunch, and say in the comment that the window exists so a task cannot be parked forever, not to detect death — a short default would turn it into the idle-based auto-release a task rail forbids. Read it from `.moe/project.json` in `applyProjectSettings` the same way the neighbouring timeouts are read, including whatever explicit-versus-default bookkeeping that function already does for them, so a project setting overrides the default and an absent setting does not clobber it. StateManager.ts, the same five sites the neighbouring timeouts use:
- `StateManagerOptions.reconcileWindowMs?: number` beside `reviewStaleTimeoutMs`.
- public `reconcileWindowMs: number` + private `reconcileWindowMsExplicit` flag.
- constructor default `options.reconcileWindowMs ?? DEFAULT_RECONCILE_WINDOW_MS`, with the justification the step asked for in a comment: the window exists so a task cannot be parked in `reconciling` FOREVER, NOT to detect death — the daemon is state-only and cannot probe a process, only the wrapper's exit trap can establish a runner stopped, and that path already closes the attempt. 2 h is far longer than a daemon restart plus runner relaunch (seconds to a minute or two) and 4x `staleWorkerTimeoutMs`, so it cannot be mistaken for a fourth idle timeout; a short default would be the idle-based auto-release a task rail forbids.

DELIBERATE DIFFERENCE FROM THE NEIGHBOURS, called out for QA: `reviewStaleTimeoutMs` is suppressed when EITHER it or `staleWorkerTimeoutMs` was given explicitly, because its default chains off `staleWorkerTimeoutMs`. `reconcileWindowMs` chains off nothing, so only its own explicit option blocks it. It also adds a positivity guard (`Number.isFinite(v) && v > 0`) the neighbours lack: a configured 0 or negative window would fire on every reconciling attempt the instant it was parked — exactly the auto-release the rail forbids — so a bad value is ignored and the default kept.

SCOPE NOTE (+1 file over the plan's five, justified): types/schema.ts `ProjectSettings` needed the optional field, or `project.settings.reconcileWindowMs` does not typecheck in `applySettingsTimeouts`. That is the same seam `reviewStaleTimeoutMs` uses (schema.ts:197). Deliberately did NOT add a `sanitizeNumber` line to persistence.ts `normalizeProject`: `normalizeProject` spreads `...project.settings` first, so an unsanitized key already survives a load/normalize/write cycle intact, whereas adding a sanitizer would write the key into EVERY project.json on every load — a board-state diff for every project that never configured it. Range safety is covered by the positivity guard above.

implementationPlan.description: WRITE THE SWEEP. In packages/moe-daemon/src/state/sweeps.ts add the exported async sweep plus its start and stop functions, following the shape read in step 1 exactly, including creating the timer through the mutex-exit wrapper and storing the handle on the state so the stop function can clear it. The sweep body: list attempts, keep ONLY those whose phase is exactly reconciling, and for each one compare the timestamp recording when it entered that phase against the configured window. Filter on the phase, never on the task's status, and never read the worker's last activity — that distinction is the whole point of the card and a task rail forbids the alternative. For an attempt past the window: close it through the store's phase setter, then release its task the way the blocked-timeout sweep does, through `nextStatusForRelease` with the assignment cleared, so the row returns to the column the existing routing chooses and a successor can claim it. The sweep NEVER opens an attempt itself; the next claim does that and the store's own exclusivity plus its generation allocator are what make the successor exactly one, so say that in a comment rather than adding a counter here. Give each attempt its own try/catch and log a failure instead of throwing, matching the per-record error handling the other sweeps use, so one unwritable record cannot stop the pass. Order the two writes so the attempt is closed before the task is released: a released task with a still-reconciling attempt would be refused to the very claimer the release just invited. Wire the start and stop calls in packages/moe-daemon/src/index.ts alongside the other sweep lifecycles, and pass the new option through wherever the sibling timeouts are passed. Re-run the focused test file; every case from step 2 must pass.

Body: `listAttempts(state)`, keep only `attempt.phase === 'reconciling'` (the PHASE, never the task's status — a reconciling attempt's task is still WORKING, so a status filter would sweep live rows), parse `attempt.lastPhaseAt` (the attempt's own clock; nothing in the sweep reads any worker's lastActivityAt), skip an unparseable timestamp rather than treating it as licence to release, and act only when `nowMs - phaseAt > state.reconcileWindowMs`.

WRITE ORDER, close then release: `setAttemptPhase(..., 'closed')` FIRST, then `updateTask(id, { assignedWorkerId: null, status: nextStatusForRelease(task, 'requeue') }, 'WORKER_TIMEOUT')`. Reversed, the row is released while its attempt is still reconciling and the sibling card's claim guard refuses it to exactly the claimer the release just invited.

'requeue', NOT the blocked sweep's 'park' — deliberate divergence from the sweep the plan pointed at. 'park' routes to BACKLOG, which is human-gated and invisible to agents, so it would yield no successor at all; 'requeue' returns WORKING-unassigned (or REVIEW when every step is done), the column the next claim reads.

The sweep opens NOTHING. A comment states why there is no counter here: openAttempt refuses a second open attempt for the same task and nextGeneration takes the max over every prior attempt including closed ones + 1, so the store already guarantees exactly one successor with a strictly greater generation. Test 7 proves that at the store level (`ATTEMPT_ALREADY_OPEN`), not just through the tool.

Per-attempt try/catch logging instead of throwing, like the neighbours; a record that fails to close stays `reconciling`, so its task is still held and a reattach still succeeds — the safe direction. Missing task (`state.getTask` null) is skipped after the close rather than throwing NOT_FOUND.

ADVERSARIAL SELF-REVIEW — read the diff as an attacker. ONE REAL DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED, TDD'd red first.

THE DEFECT: the sweep released the task on the attempt's age alone, without checking WHO holds the row now. A dangling reconciling attempt whose task has since been handed to another worker would have yanked that worker's live work — a straight violation of "never yank a live worker". Fixed: `if (task.assignedWorkerId && task.assignedWorkerId !== attempt.workerId) continue;` after the close, so the stale attempt is still closed (right) but the current owner keeps its row (also right). New case "closes a stale attempt but never yanks a row a different worker now holds" failed first with `AssertionError: expected null to be 'worker-Z'`, then passed. Fixture note for anyone extending it: `updateTask` throws `Task already assigned to <id>` on a direct reassign — unassign to null first.

CHECKLIST, each verified against the diff rather than recalled:
- CLOCK: the window is compared only against `attempt.lastPhaseAt`. `lastActivityAt` appears 3 times in the new sweep body — two comments and ONE WRITE that passes the stored value straight back to `updateWorker` so it does not stamp a fresh one. Nothing reads it for any decision, threshold or comparison. No idle-based auto-release reached WORKING or PLANNING.
- FILTER: `attempt.phase !== 'reconciling'` continue — the phase exactly, never the task's status. running (incl. reattached) and finalizing untouched however old; two dedicated cases at WINDOW*10.
- BOUNDARY: `nowMs - phaseAt <= state.reconcileWindowMs` continue, so it fires only strictly past, matching the neighbours' `>`. The WINDOW-1 case asserts whole-record equality, so an always-fire sweep fails it.
- ORDER: `setAttemptPhase(closed)` precedes `updateTask`, so the release never invites a claimer the reconciling hold refuses.
- SUCCESSOR: the sweep calls no openAttempt. Repeated pass writes nothing — asserted by whole-record equality AND file mtime, plus `listAttempts` length unchanged. Store-level exclusivity proven via `ATTEMPT_ALREADY_OPEN`.
- ERROR HANDLING: per-attempt try/catch logging, not throwing; a failed close leaves the attempt reconciling, so its task stays held and a reattach still works — the safe direction. Proven with a stubbed `writeEntity` failure that does not stop the pass.
- TIMER: armed via `state.mutex.exit(() => setInterval(...))`, `.unref()`ed, handle on the state; the stop case spies `clearInterval` and asserts it got THAT handle and the field is cleared.
- UNTOUCHED: sweeps.ts has exactly ONE deleted line in the whole diff — the import statement it replaces. The REVIEW self-heal, the stale-worker watcher, the dependency unblock, the resource reaper and the Layer-3 prune are byte-identical.
- Unparseable/missing `lastPhaseAt` is skipped, not treated as licence to release. A deleted task is skipped after the close instead of throwing NOT_FOUND. Iteration is over a snapshot array, so mutating `state.attempts` mid-pass is safe. The whole pass runs under one `mutex.runExclusive`, so no tool handler can interleave a reattach at an await boundary.

SCOPE: 5 files, as the plan budgeted — but a different 5. `types/schema.ts` is IN (the `ProjectSettings` field, without which `project.settings.reconcileWindowMs` does not typecheck; same seam `reviewStaleTimeoutMs` uses) and `src/index.ts` is OUT, because it wires no sweeps and no timeouts (evidence in the step-1 note; all three existing sweep lifecycles live in `StateManager.load()`/`clearEmitter()`, which is where this one went). No process probing added: grep of the daemon diff for child_process / execSync / spawn( / process.kill returns NONE. No forbidden patterns (eval(, innerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, __proto__): 0 hits. Startup reconciliation, the reattach tool and the claim hold were left entirely to the sibling card — `attemptStore.ts`, `claimNextTask.ts`, `reattachAttempt.ts` and `index.ts` have zero changed lines.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered: (1) Implementing a confirmed-dead probe in the daemon: rejected outright by an epic rail that keeps the daemon state-only and never a process actor. The only authority that can establish a process stopped is the wrapper's exit trap calling deregister, and the attempt-lifecycle work already closes the attempt on that path, so the first definition-of-done item is met by the existing path plus this card's window. Step 1 verifies that the deregister close covers a reconciling attempt and the completion summary states it, so QA is not left guessing. (2) Adding a successor counter to the sweep: rejected, and worth naming because it looks like the obvious way to satisfy 'exactly one successor'. The store already guarantees it — the sweep never opens an attempt, the next claim does, the generation allocator takes the maximum over every prior attempt plus one, and openAttempt refuses a second open attempt for the same task. A counter here would be a second source of truth for a rule that already holds. (3) Measuring the window from the worker's last activity: forbidden by a task rail and by the sibling's acceptance fixture, whose worker is quiet for three hours and must keep its task. The measurement is the attempt's own phase timestamp. (4) Filtering on task status rather than attempt phase: rejected, since a reconciling attempt's task is still WORKING and a status filter would sweep live rows. (5) Releasing the task before closing the attempt: rejected — the reconciling claim hold from the sibling card would refuse the very claimer the release just invited, so the close comes first.
planningNotes.codebaseInsights: sweeps.ts already holds three sweeps in one consistent shape: a start function that stores its handle on the state and builds the timer through `state.mutex.exit(() => setInterval(...))`, a matching stop function, and a separately exported async sweep a test can call directly with no timer at all. The mutex-exit wrapper is load-bearing: a timer created inside the mutex context inherits it and its callback would run unlocked. runBlockedTimeoutSweep around line 213 is the model for releasing a task from a sweep, and it routes through nextStatusForRelease rather than writing a status directly, which this sweep must also do. The settings seam is three places in StateManager.ts — the option on StateManagerOptions near line 345, the constructor default near line 436, and applyProjectSettings near line 1079, which carries explicit-versus-default bookkeeping worth mirroring — and one table row in docs/CONFIGURATION.md near line 177. The attempt store needs no change at all for this card: setAttemptPhase already treats closed as terminal and a repeated phase as a no-op, currentAttempt already ignores closed attempts, and the generation allocator already takes the maximum over every prior attempt including closed ones. That is why this plan is five files rather than seven.
planningNotes.risks: The defect that would pass review is applying the window to the wrong phase or the wrong clock: filtering on task status sweeps live rows, and measuring from the worker's last activity reintroduces exactly the idle-based auto-release two rails forbid. Both have dedicated tests, including a boundary case one millisecond inside the window, because an always-fire sweep passes every past-the-window assertion. Write ordering matters: closing after releasing leaves a window where the released task is refused to its new claimer by the sibling card's reconciling hold. Adding an interval to the startup path touches every test that boots the daemon, and an uncleared timer surfaces as a hanging or flaky suite rather than a clean failure, so verify the stop function actually clears it. The named verification command includes a file the sibling card creates; if that card has not landed, report it honestly rather than stubbing the file. Finally, be honest about what the window is: releasing on a timer alone does not prove the old runner stopped. If it is alive and merely slow, its next daemon mutation is refused as superseded, and containing its file writes is outside the daemon's reach — the epic's own architecture notes say so and the completion summary should repeat it.
